blogs.name: Simon Willison's Weblog
blogs.title: Quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang
blogs.description: We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is…
blogs.content:
We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"

 Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.

 Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.

 — Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang , How the Claude Code team does code review

 Tags: anthropic , claude , ai , claude-code , llms , addy-osmani , coding-agents , generative-ai , agentic-engineering , code-review

blogs.title: LaTeX renderer
blogs.description: Tool: LaTeX renderer Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office, which provides a suite of web app…
blogs.content:
Tool: LaTeX renderer

 Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office , which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner).

 Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link.

 It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works:

 Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used:

 I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too.

 Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks:

 Safe from XSS? We could run in an iframe sandbox like we do on the SVG markdown render project

 I had it copy the Gist/URL loading feature from that tool as well:

 We should have an option to load latex from a URL (or gist) similar to the markdown SVG tool

 Here's an example link . The tool uses Pako 2.1.0 , MathJax 4.1.3 , faster-latex 0.3.1 , and DOMPurify 3.4.16 .

 Tags: latex , paul-ford , tools , urls , ai , generative-ai , llms

blogs.content:
( X: @twostraws )

 Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery!

 As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone . Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings .

 On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week.

 What is Apple Doing? On last week’s Dithering, John and I bemoaned Apple’s exit from home appliances in the 2010s; now the company is back and John doesn’t see the point . I think a big problem was Apple’s marketing video; after I explained what Apple was trying to accomplish on Sharp Tech Andrew was almost persuaded to go all in on HomeView. — Ben Thompson

 SpaceX Continues Eating and Expands Its Appetite.  Elon Musk and SpaceX have continued their spectrum buying spree, and in Tuesday’s update Ben broke down the implications of both the latest deal, as well as recent deals that mobile carriers (and airlines) have done to avoid reliance on SpaceX. This market’s dynamics are fascinating to me, and for SpaceX, what once looked like a play to become the de-facto provider of emergency satellite coverage among mobile providers now looks like a company that’s coming for primary cellular coverage. Come to read about the methods that could make that path viable, and stay to appreciate challenges that make it a quintessential Musk strategy.  — Andrew Sharp

 Titles, Takes, and the Washington Wizards.  The NBA season begins next Tuesday, and if you want to have a good time preparing this weekend, we’ve got you covered. First, Greatest of All Talk makes the case for eight different potential title winners (although I must warn you that our Knicks repeat case was extremely unconvincing) and runs down our favorite highlights from the preseason. Then, for Friday’s Sharp Text , I played the most dangerous game of all and expressed confidence the Washington Wizards (for the first time in a full decade) while also offering 18 more takes and predictions for the rest of the league. — AS

---
